title: The Golden Mango

full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya’s elderly mother was pious and charitable. One summer afternoon, she expressed a sudden craving for ripe, sweet mangoes. The King immediately ordered a basket of the finest fruit from the countryside, but before the basket could arrive, the queen mother fell suddenly ill and passed away peacefully.

The King was overcome with intense grief and filial remorse, weeping that his mother's final earthly wish for a mango had gone unfulfilled.

Hearing of the King’s emotional vulnerability, the chief palace priests saw a golden opportunity to enrich themselves. They assembled before the mourning monarch and solemnly pronounced:
'Maharaj, your mother's soul cannot attain eternal tranquility until her unfulfilled desire is expiated through sacred charity. According to our ancestral scriptures, you must craft thirty mangoes of solid gold, each weighing fifty tolas, and distribute them to thirty learned priests along with bags of silver!'

Grief-stricken, the King readily agreed and ordered the royal goldsmiths to forge the thirty solid gold mangoes.

When Tenali Raman heard of this shameless exploitation, his blood boiled at the priests' greed.
Tenali sent a private messenger to the thirty priests:
'Revered scholars, today my late mother’s memorial anniversary also falls. I desire to offer you sacred gifts to fulfill her last unfulfilled wish. Come to my courtyard immediately after the palace distribution.'

The greedy priests were overjoyed at the thought of receiving double charity in a single day.
After collecting their heavy gold mangoes from the palace, they hurried straight to Tenali’s house.

Tenali welcomed them with excessive courtesy into his enclosed courtyard, bolted the heavy wooden gates, and summoned his two burly servants, who held glowing red-hot iron branding rods pulled from a charcoal furnace!

The priests leaped back in terror: 'Tenali! What madness is this? Why hast thou brought branding irons?'

Tenali replied with tearful solemnity:
'Revered priests, in her final days, my poor mother suffered from agonizing chronic rheumatism in her legs. The royal physicians advised that the only cure was to brand her thighs with red-hot iron rods. Alas, she died before the treatment could be applied!
Her final wish remains unfulfilled! As learned scholars, you know that whatever was unfulfilled in this life must be received by the priests on her behalf! Come, roll up your dhoyas, so my servants may brand each of you with three strokes of the glowing iron to release my mother’s soul!'

The terrified priests shrieked in horror:
'Mercy, Tenali! Are you insane? Branding with red-hot irons will burn our skin to ashes!'

Tenali glared at them with righteous fury:
'Why, holy men? If the King’s mother wished for a juicy fruit and you demanded solid gold mangoes, then when my mother wished for hot iron branding, surely hot iron rods are the only appropriate gift!'

Realizing they had been caught in their own trap of religious extortion, the humiliated priests dropped their thirty solid gold mangoes onto the courtyard stones and fled out the back gate!

Tenali gathered the thirty gold mangoes, carried them back to the King, and revealed the priests' deceit.
King Krishnadevaraya hugged Tenali with tears of relief, realizing that true filial piety is honored by honest deeds, not by feeding the boundless greed of impostors.
moral: Greedy opportunists who exploit religious rites for personal gain deserve a taste of their own medicine.
